chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated: Some of our companions narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Abu Wahb, from Muhammad ibn Masnun, who said: I asked him (meaning Abu Abdillah)...

...about the saying of Allah: 'And when they commit an indecency, they say: We found our fathers doing this, and Allah has enjoined it on us. Say: Surely Allah does not enjoin indecency; do you say against Allah what you do not know?'

He said: Have you seen anyone claiming that Allah ordered him to commit adultery, drink wine, or do any of these forbidden things? I said: No. He said: Then what is this indecency that they claim Allah ordered them to do? I said: Allah and His guardian are more aware. He said: This is among the followers of the Imams of injustice; they claimed that Allah ordered them to follow some people, whom Allah had never ordered them to follow. So Allah denied their saying and informed them that they had fabricated lies against Him, and He called that from among them an indecency.

key_terms.الِائْتِمَاء: To follow or take as an imam/leader

ai.seo_question: What does the term 'fahisha' (indecency) refer to in the context of the verse about following ancestors' sins?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Kitab al-Ghayba*, Imam al-Sadiq (as) interprets the 'indecency' (fahsha) in Surah Al-A'raf not merely as specific sins like adultery, but as the theological error of blind imitation (taqlid) of unjust leaders. He contextualizes this within the Shia discourse on the Imams of Injustice, arguing that their followers falsely attributed divine command to their own erroneous practices, thereby committing a lie against Allah. This highlights the Shia principle that true obedience is limited to what Allah explicitly commanded, rejecting the presumption of authority by unjust figures.
